subject: Chemistry
title: Thomson Discovers the Electron
description: A short lesson to help you apply Thomson Discovers the Electron.

hook.text: In 1897, J.J. Thomson found that atoms aren't indivisible. They contain tiny negative particles—electrons.

buildup.text: He shot cathode rays through electric and magnetic fields. The rays bent, proving they were charged particles.

discovery.text: He calculated the charge-to-mass ratio and found these particles were 1,800 times lighter than hydrogen atoms.

twist.text: He proposed the 'plum pudding model': electrons embedded in a positive sphere, like raisins in a pudding.

climax.text: Thomson was wrong about the model—but right about the electron. He won the Nobel Prize in 1906.

punchline.text: Atoms have parts. The first subatomic particle was found in a glass tube.

quiz.question: How did Thomson discover the electron?
options: He showed cathode rays were tiny charged particles deflected by electric fields
He split atoms using radioactive bombardment
He observed electrons orbiting atoms under a microscope

details.summary: In 1897 J.J. Thomson discovered the electron by deflecting cathode rays with electric and magnetic fields, proving that atoms contain smaller negatively charged particles. His plum pudding model proposed electrons embedded in a positively charged mass like raisins in a cake.
details.whyItMatters: Thomson shattered the idea that atoms are indivisible, opening the era of subatomic physics. The electron was the first fundamental particle ever discovered.
takeaways: Thomson used cathode ray tubes to discover negatively charged electrons
His plum pudding model was the first subatomic structure proposal
The discovery proved atoms have internal structure and are not solid

faq.question: How did Thomson determine the charge-to-mass ratio of the electron?
faq.answer: He measured how much cathode rays deflected under known electric and magnetic fields. By balancing the two forces, he calculated the charge-to-mass ratio and found it was over a thousand times larger than for hydrogen ions, meaning electrons were incredibly light.

faq.question: Why was the plum pudding model eventually replaced?
faq.answer: Rutherford's 1911 gold foil experiment showed that most alpha particles passed through atoms undeflected, while a few bounced back sharply. This proved the positive charge was concentrated in a tiny dense nucleus, not spread diffusely as Thomson's model predicted.
